title: Rama's anger
hook: Rama's patience runs out, and the Gita's chain of anger
carry: krodha clouds memory: remember the friend

segments.voice: Yesterday: the rains ended, and Hanuman's reminder: kama is a real aim, but dharma comes first.

No messenger. Not yesterday, not today. Rama looks down the mountain toward the city where his friend is enjoying a throne Rama won for him. He doesn't know about Hanuman's reminder or the orders that went out. All he sees is a clear road and a silent city. His patience, which has held through grief and rain, finally gives way. Valmiki lets us hear all of it.
screen: `NO MESSENGER.` → `A SILENT CITY BELOW.` → `PATIENCE GIVES WAY.`

segments.voice: Rama speaks to Lakshmana, first in grief, then in anger. The time we agreed on is here, he says, and Sugriva hasn't come. He thinks I'm a man without a kingdom, someone he can forget. So Rama gives Lakshmana a message to carry, and it isn't subtle: the path Vali took is not closed. Keep your word, or follow Vali. The word for what Sugriva let slip is samaya: an agreement, and also an appointed time. Then watch Lakshmana. Rama is angry; Lakshmana is angrier. He wants to go down and kill Sugriva today. So Rama, even while sending him, holds him back: don't kill him. Speak gently first. Remind him of the friendship. The Bhagavad Gita traces how anger runs, like a chain. Dwell on something and attachment grows; from attachment, desire; from desire, anger; from anger, confusion; from confusion, memory slips; and when memory goes, judgment goes with it. Hindu teachers count krodha, anger, among the six inner enemies. Many teachers read that lost memory as forgetting who someone is to you. Rama's anger is fair, and he still breaks the chain where it counts: he doesn't lose his memory of the friendship. He keeps his judgment, and keeps his brother on the reins. Lakshmana, left alone, might have run the chain to the end. It meets a life now in the angry text you're about to send. Rama's story doesn't pretend anger never comes. The Gita shows where it leads if you follow it: so stop before it steals your memory of who that person is to you. Lakshmana picks up his bow and walks down the mountain.
screen: `THE PATH VALI TOOK IS NOT CLOSED.` · `SPEAK GENTLY FIRST.` · `GITA 2.62–63: THE CHAIN OF ANGER.` · `RAMA KEEPS THE MEMORY.` · then, large: `REMEMBER THE FRIEND.`

segments.voice: Recall someone who let you down. Breathe in and feel the anger honestly, where it sits in your body. Breathe out slowly, and bring to mind one good thing that person has been to you: the kind of memory, many teachers say, that anger steals. If you pray, say Om shanti three times, the words that close so many Hindu prayers. If not, take three slow breaths out.
Lakshmana's warning. Rama's hard message, sent in anger that still remembers the friend.
Your line: krodha clouds memory: remember the friend. Rama was angry, and he still remembered. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 591 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TARA AT THE PALACE DOOR.`

howItsDone: The Bhagavad Gita (2.62–63) traces the chain from desire to anger to confusion and lost judgment, and Hindu teachers count anger (krodha) among the six inner enemies; storytellers use Rama's message to Sugriva to talk about anger that stays in bounds.

samaya.meaning: an agreement, and also an appointed time

Vali.meaning: Sugriva's elder brother, once king of Kishkindha

Sugriva.meaning: the monkey king, Vali's younger brother, Rama's ally

Lakshmana.meaning: Rama's younger brother, beside him in exile

krodha.meaning: anger; one of the six inner enemies
